I appreciate the opportunity to comment on CMS-0062-P, â€˜Medicare and 
Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care  Plans, State Medicaid 
Agencies, Childrenâ€™s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the 
Federally-Facilitated Exchangesâ€.
For the splitting of the proposed requirements for drug prior 
authorization into those for the â€˜medical benefitâ€™ and â€˜pharmacy benefitâ€™ 
these are vague terms. I like the idea tying these to how the claim would 
be submitted, though sometimes claims for drugs are submitted to the wrong 
entity and have to be resubmitted using the other method. I would imagine 
the same could happen here even if the definitions point to the manner of 
how a claim for this drug would be submitted to the payer.
In regards to the naming a required FHIR standards, the base FHIR 
standard does need to be named in regulation to keep everything level. 
Many of the Resources in FHIR R4 are not defined within a profile under US 
Core or any of the proposed Implementation Guides (IGs) so in order to 
have a definition, the FHIR base standard needs to be included. Another 
item is that an IG does not spell out definitions for all Resources which 
might be needed, or are Referenced within its profiles. All Resource do 
not even have a US Core profile either.
This brings up an issue about a future transition for FHIR base 
standard. It is not clear how the transition between R versions of base 
FHIR would look when dealing with Resources which could be being used in 
different versions due to different IGs. Since many of the Resources in R4 
are still not Normative, they could have some changes where as an R4 
version they might not be compliant in say R6. This will make it quite a 
challenge if you have Resources created under R4 and have to use them 
under say R6 to be compliant. You would have either created them, or 
received them, under R4 but then need to convey them at a time that R6 is 
the named version. This is unlike how this would occur under X12 where 
messages are tied to versions and are not bundled together at a future 
date to create an interoperable 'unit'. With payers and possibly providers 
receiving Resources from other covered entities, they would likely be 
keeping them as they were received and would be required to pass them 
along in the future. These Resources would be compliant with the R version 
they were originally created under but might not be compliant with a 
future R version of FHIR. This could also occur with changes in the 
version of an IG.  At which time the base FHIR version changes there will 
need to be guidance and a process on how to handle Resources which were 
created under an earlier version but need to be sent under the new 
version, especially if there are significant (or breaking) changes to the 
Resource.
In regards to if it would be helpful for payers to have specific 
capabilities of required IGs be identified, I would agree with this. In 
the example on SMART, if there were no specific capabilities identified to 
be named in regulation, then payers would seem to have to be able to meet 
everything that is listed in the IG, even if it is not relevant to the 
required APIs.
For the requiring of the CARIN guide for Provider Access and Payer-to-
Payer, I do not see how this could be named in regulation as a requirement 
especially since the current version of the CARIN IG for Blue Button 
(2.2.0) states that 'This IG addresses consumer access to claims and 
encounter data and does not directly address these other APIs.'. How can 
this be named in regulation as a requirement when it does not meet the 
requirements for the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs?
For the recommending of the FAST Security IG for registration, 
authentication and authorization, this may be recommended but we will be 
using what our Risk office and Legal Department require of us to protect 
our systems and be compliant with Federal and State laws & Regulations and 
internal policies. And for how much testing would be necessary to propose 
using the FAST Security IG, I would say only when it has been used in 
Production and all of the liability exposure has been sorted out  via laws 
and case law (and covered by cybersecurity insurance).
As for working with trust communities, I am not sure we can have a trust 
community that we just accept anyone who comes to our door stating they 
are from 'this community'. There does seem to be some liability exposure 
if we do not do our Due Diligence upon anyone approaching us. This is not 
any different from a X12 or NCPDP direct connection request.
In regards to adding real-time prescription drug cost and coverage 
information to the Patient Access API, HHS should wait and see about 
having people use what has already been built before building out 
additional features that might be of limited value to patients. Also 
payers would likely only build support for RTPBC IG if it is required, not 
just if it is recommended. They currently only have time, budget and 
people to meet required things, not â€œnice to haveâ€ or â€œwouldnâ€™t it be nice 
if we had one of theseâ€.
For the decision timeframe for prior authorizations, the measure of â€œas 
the enrollees health condition requiresâ€ is hard to measure or audit 
against. Is this a flag of some sort in the API request or is it something 
to be inferred based upon the diagnosis and services requested?
For the additional non-drug prior authorization measures which payers 
need to report, this seems to be acceptable.
For requiring a specific reason to be supplied for drug prior 
authorization denials, there is no code list specified. This needs to be 
named so that everyone is working off of the same list, not payer-specific 
lists.
In regards to the proposals about collecting payer FHIR endpoints, some 
payers only want to make public their registration endpoint and then would 
supply the relevant endpoint(s) to those who are registered and as would 
be appropriate for what they have registered for. I can also see there 
being a challenge in how a payer endpoint directory will be accessed. Each 
payer will organize their endpoints to how they feel it is best for their 
particular circumstances. When trying to access or organize this list, CMS 
could face a similar issue they came across with how payers enumerated 
themselves under HPID/OEID. It was not a one size fits all arrangement and 
ended up being quite a mess. I can foresee this being a similar situation 
for a payer endpoint directory unless there is some guidance from CMS on 
how it should be organized.
For the proposed Provider Access API statistics, this should be kept 
very simple until everyone has experience with how it gets used to know 
what might be collectible and relevant. This would be similar to how 
Patient Access Api statistics were not required until the API had been in 
use for a period of time.
In regards to the removal of the drug formulary from the Provider Access 
and Payer to Payer APIs, I agree this should be done as they do not seem 
to be relevant for these APIs.
For the changes to the named HIPAA Standard Transactions, I disagree 
with the proposals. The 278 for Prior Authorization, though not used as 
much as the claims 837s which is proper for it to be used less as there 
are fewer prior authorization requests than there are claims and 
encounters, are still used in some way in over half of all prior 
authorization requests as per the recent CAQH Indexes. If somehow CMS were 
to still name the CRD/DTR/PAS as the HIPAA Standard Transactions for Prior 
Authorization, then they should also allow for an enforcement discretion, 
or some other mechanism, to allow for the 278 to still be used for those 
who use it today and find that it works for them. They should not be 
forced to change what works for willing trading partners, in the same way 
that currently willing trading partners can exchange FHIR transactions for 
Prior Authorization if that works for them.
For the proposed changes to the 270/271, this make no sense. This is a 
very well used transaction as it is now. It can supply information about 
the need for a prior authorization when returning other information in a 
response to an inquiry. In the upcoming 8060 version of the 270/271 there 
is even more details about prior authorization that have been built in and 
are ready to be used when this is named. The proposed change in definition 
to split hairs about when to use a 270/271 and when to use CRD seems to be 
hard to decipher and does not provide any guidance on what this means to 
one of the most used Standard Transactions. Does the proposed change in 
definition and what the 270/271 can convey mean that no prior 
authorization data can be returned in a 271? How would this affect 
providers? It would seem that then they will have to do a 270/271 and then 
a CRD to get the information that they can get now, or in an even better 
way under 8060 in the future for not only Prior Authorizations but also 
referrals and certifications. The 270/271 should be left alone to do what 
it does well now and will do even better under 8060. If HHS still wants to 
go down the path of naming the CRD as a Standard Transaction, then they 
should come up with a distinct named transaction for it and leave the 
current definition and specification for the 270/271 alone.
As for the timing of making any of these changes to the HIPAA Standard 
Transactions, consideration should be given to how these changes would 
align, or not align, with a compliance date for 8060. If the date is prior 
to 8060 then changes would have to be made while under 5010 to existing 
working processes.
For referrals, this should not be included as a named function of the 
CRD/DTR/PAS. This is not the main purpose of these transactions nor does 
it seem to have been a focus of use in production for many to prove that 
it works. This also has a well-established base of use for another 278 and 
should be kept either as-is (not named) or should be considered for naming 
this 278 as a Standard Transaction under 8060 since it is used in 
Production.
As for whether to consider using HL7â€™s Major.Minor.Patch versioning to 
allow for maintenance changes which do not require rulemaking, this should 
not be allowed. FHIR IGs should have to follow the same path as the other 
SDOs do for having changes to their guides be named. As many more entities 
are having to use these guide, changes have to be accommodated and worked 
on to meet changes in compliance.
In regards to testing to ensure compliance with implementation guides, a 
challenge of testing with Inferno, or any external testing site, is how to 
prevent PHI/PII exposure if the payer test system only contains real data 
(not synthetic) so then they could not use Inferno as an app.
For the proposal to recommend the ATR IG for exchanging member 
attribution, I am not sure this guide is fully established yet. There also 
does not seem to be a limitation in who can exchange or request this 
exchange. If this guide is to be recommended, it should be limited to only 
in-network providers the same way as Provider Access is limited.
In regards to the question of â€˜Whether any of these IGs are now mature 
and important enough for CMS to adopt in a final rule.â€™ I would say that 
we have not had enough experience with a large enough base to know that 
any of these IGs are mature enough to be adopted. In comparison to when 
X12 was named for Standard Transactions, X12 transactions had been being 
used for well over a decade in various industries so the data structures 
and exchange principles had been well proven in Production. This is not 
the case with these IGs.
For the question about direct data entry, this exception should be 
maintained as it is used only by those who want or need it, and it is 
essentially the â€˜break glassâ€™ method when all else fails.
I thank you again for this opportunity to comment on CMS-0062-P and look 
forward to seeing all of this Proposed Rule, with some minor 
clarifications I offered above, be moved forward as the Final Rule.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Not stated
- **Stakeholder type:** Individual / Payer or health IT technical stakeholder
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** No formal credentials stated; the comment references payer endpoint practices, risk/legal review, production implementation, X12/NCPDP connections, and compliance testing.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The commenter generally supports moving the proposed rule forward but requests substantial technical clarifications and opposes key HIPAA transaction changes. The comment focuses on FHIR versioning, IG maturity, endpoint reporting, denial-code standardization, privacy/security liability, API metric scope, and preserving X12 278 and 270/271 workflows alongside or instead of CRD/DTR/PAS as HIPAA standards.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations; references CMS-0062-P and HIPAA Standard Transactions.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR R4 and possible R6; US Core; Da Vinci CRD/DTR/PAS; CARIN IG for Blue Button 2.2.0; FAST Security IG; RTPBC IG; HL7 versioning; X12 278, 270/271, 837, 5010, and 8060; NCPDP; Inferno; ATR IG; SMART.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Medical vs Pharmacy Benefit Definitions**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Tying the distinction to claim submission method may help, but claims can be sent to the wrong entity and resubmitted through another path.
- **Specific request:** Clarify how benefit-category definitions work when drug claims move between medical and pharmacy submission workflows.

**Topic 2: Required FHIR Standards and Version Transitions**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** IGs and US Core do not define every referenced FHIR resource, many R4 resources are not normative, and future R-version transitions could create incompatibility for stored or received resources.
- **Specific request:** Name the base FHIR standard in regulation, identify required IG capabilities, provide transition guidance for base FHIR and IG version changes, and do not rely on HL7 Major.Minor.Patch updates outside rulemaking.

**Topic 3: IG Suitability, Security, Trust, and Testing**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / PRIVACY-SECURITY / ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Clarify / Oppose in part
- **Rationale:** CARIN Blue Button says it addresses consumer access rather than Provider Access or Payer-to-Payer; FAST Security and trust communities raise risk, legal, due diligence, and liability issues; Inferno testing can expose PHI/PII when synthetic test data is unavailable.
- **Specific request:** Do not require unsuitable IGs; allow security decisions consistent with risk/legal obligations; require adequate production experience and liability clarity; solve PHI/PII testing issues.

**Topic 4: API Endpoint Reporting, Metrics, and Formulary Data**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify / Support in part
- **Rationale:** Payers may only want public registration endpoints; CMS endpoint directories need organization guidance; Provider Access API statistics should remain simple until usage patterns mature.
- **Specific request:** Provide endpoint-directory organization guidance, keep Provider Access API metrics simple initially, and remove drug formulary from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 5: Decision Timeframes and Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** The phrase "as the enrollee's health condition requires" is hard to measure or audit, and payer-specific denial reason lists would undermine standardization.
- **Specific request:** Define how urgency is represented or inferred in API requests and specify a standard code list for drug PA denial reasons.

**Topic 6: HIPAA Prior Authorization Transaction Standards**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Oppose / Modify
- **Rationale:** X12 278 is still used in more than half of PA requests according to recent CAQH Indexes; 270/271 is widely used for eligibility and PA-related information; referrals have existing 278 usage; CRD/DTR/PAS production maturity is not proven.
- **Specific request:** Do not replace or redefine established X12 workflows; if CRD/DTR/PAS are named, allow enforcement discretion or another mechanism for willing trading partners to continue using 278; leave 270/271 intact or create a distinct CRD transaction; align timing with X12 8060.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** The commenter supports naming required standards only with clear scope, including the base FHIR standard and specific required IG capabilities.
- **S2-S3:** The commenter asks CMS to clarify base FHIR and IG version transitions, especially for resources created under earlier FHIR versions.
- **S6:** The commenter opposes requiring CARIN Blue Button 2.2.0 for Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer because the IG says it does not directly address those APIs.
- **S12:** The comment identifies technical challenges for medical-benefit drug PA, including claim routing and benefit-category ambiguity.
- **S15:** The commenter directly asks for clarification of medical versus pharmacy benefit terms.
- **S16-S17:** The commenter supports requiring denial reasons only if CMS names a standard code list instead of allowing payer-specific lists.
- **S20:** The commenter asks CMS to clarify how "as the enrollee's health condition requires" can be measured or audited.
- **S23-S27:** The commenter raises endpoint reporting concerns, including public exposure of only registration endpoints and the need for CMS guidance on endpoint directory organization.
- **S29-S35:** The commenter says Provider Access API statistics should remain simple until industry has experience with actual usage.
- **S44:** The commenter opposes naming CRD/DTR/PAS as HIPAA prior authorization standards at this time.
- **S46:** The commenter asks CMS to preserve X12 278 use for willing trading partners and not disturb existing 270/271 functionality.
- **S47:** The commenter asks CMS to align any HIPAA transaction changes with the X12 8060 compliance date.
- **S50:** The commenter states that the relevant IGs lack enough broad production experience to be considered mature enough for adoption.
- **S53-S55:** The commenter recommends enforcement discretion or a similar mechanism if CMS finalizes CRD/DTR/PAS as HIPAA PA standards.
- **S54:** The commenter raises testing concerns about Inferno or external testing tools when payer test environments contain PHI/PII.
- **S60-S63:** The commenter opposes allowing HL7 Major.Minor.Patch maintenance changes without rulemaking and asks that FHIR IG changes follow the same process as other SDO guides.
- **S65:** The commenter compares FHIR IG maturity unfavorably with X12's long production history before HIPAA adoption.
- **GENERAL/RFI:** The commenter asks CMS to retain the direct data entry exception as a break-glass method and to limit ATR IG member attribution exchange to in-network providers if recommended.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Clarify medical-benefit and pharmacy-benefit definitions for drug PA when claims are routed or resubmitted differently.
2. Name the base FHIR standard in regulation, not only IGs.
3. Identify specific required IG capabilities instead of requiring every capability in an IG.
4. Provide clear guidance for transitions across FHIR R versions and IG versions.
5. Do not require CARIN Blue Button for APIs it does not address.
6. Treat FAST Security IG and trust-community participation as subject to payer risk, legal, compliance, liability, and due diligence requirements.
7. Wait before adding RTPBC to the Patient Access API unless it is required and demonstrably useful.
8. Define how urgent PA timing based on the enrollee's condition is represented and audited.
9. Specify a standard code list for drug PA denial reasons.
10. Provide guidance for organizing CMS's payer endpoint directory.
11. Keep Provider Access API metrics simple until use is better understood.
12. Remove drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
13. Do not name CRD/DTR/PAS as HIPAA PA standards now; preserve X12 278 and 270/271 workflows.
14. Align any HIPAA transaction changes with X12 8060.
15. Do not include referrals as a named CRD/DTR/PAS function.
16. Require rulemaking for FHIR IG maintenance changes.
17. Address PHI/PII risks in external IG testing.
18. Limit ATR IG exchange to in-network providers if recommended.
19. Maintain the direct data entry exception.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Ambiguous benefit definitions, FHIR and IG version instability, unsuitable IG mandates, security liability, endpoint directory complexity, auditability of timelines, nonstandard denial codes, immature IGs, and disruption of X12 workflows.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Compliance confusion, resource incompatibility across FHIR versions, overbroad IG implementation burden, PHI/PII exposure in testing, payer endpoint directory disorder, duplicative 270/271 plus CRD workflows, and forced replacement of working 278 trading partner arrangements.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Limited time, budget, and staff; non-synthetic test data; risk/legal requirements; production maturity gaps; X12 5010/8060 timing; diverse payer endpoint organization models.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Recent CAQH Indexes reportedly show X12 278 is used in some way in over half of prior authorization requests.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CAQH Indexes; no formal citation details provided.
- **Examples provided:** Claims submitted to the wrong entity and resubmitted; FHIR R4 resources later needing exchange under R6; CARIN Blue Button 2.2.0 scope statement; HPID/OEID enumeration problems; 270/271 PA-related information; Inferno testing with real data; direct data entry as break-glass workflow.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Payers, providers, trading partners, health IT vendors, CMS, regulators, risk/legal teams, trust communities, and patients indirectly affected by workflow disruption.
- **Economic implications:** The commenter cites limited payer time, budget, and staffing and warns against requiring nice-to-have features or duplicative workflow changes.
- **Technical feasibility:** Mixed; the commenter views some API and FHIR proposals as feasible only with clearer versioning, capability scoping, testing protections, and production maturity.
- **Patient care impact:** Indirect; clearer standards and preserving working transactions could prevent operational disruption, while denial-code and timeline clarity could improve PA processing.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Concerned
- **Tone:** Technical and critical
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "the base FHIR standard does need to be named in regulation" - Context: Commenter's FHIR standards recommendation.
2. "there will need to be guidance and a process" - Context: FHIR version transition concern.
3. "there is no code list specified" - Context: Drug PA denial reason standardization concern.
4. "The 270/271 should be left alone" - Context: Opposition to proposed HIPAA transaction redefinition.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The commenter asks CMS to align HIPAA changes with X12 8060 and clarify version transitions.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment notes payers have limited time, budget, and staff for required work.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - FAST Security, trust communities, PHI/PII testing exposure, and liability are major concerns.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment is primarily focused on whether proposed standards can be implemented reliably.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The commenter questions FHIR IG maturity and compares it to X12's production history.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - The comment discusses what should be named in regulation and whether maintenance updates should bypass rulemaking.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment discusses payer-provider-trading partner connections, trust communities, and CMS endpoint directory coordination.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - The commenter asks CMS to clarify vague benefit categories and claim-submission edge cases.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment supports standardized denial code lists and endpoint organization guidance.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The commenter strongly emphasizes preserving X12 278, 270/271, referrals, and direct data entry workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Implementation guide, Inferno, ATR, SMART, RTPBC, and versioning issues affect vendors and testing infrastructure.
